## Session 2026-10-11 — Index version 68: the text a section prints at its own level has a row, and Browse lists it first (#1536)

Pull request C of the index bump (`Planning/Index-Bump-Brief-2026-10-11.md`, §3.2; decision 1), begun on the owner's word after #1639 merged, in the session that wrote the brief and pull requests A and B. Index version 68, so every library re-indexes once at the build that carries the bump. No CloudKit deploy, no `@Model` or stored property, no table or column, no bundled file. The owner also asked for the two Mac walks that were owed, #1576's lane 5 and #1577's lane 2; they are at the end of this entry.

**The defect.** A `<div>` that is neither a document nor a section the index promotes passes what it holds to the division around it, and at the root that is dropped. A section that holds documents was never promoted, so the text printed at its own level reached nothing: the list of those present above a meeting's minutes, a treaty's signature and ratification dates under its title, the statement of a case above the documents filed with it.

**What was built**
- **The parse** (`TEIParserDelegate.sectionDecision`, `ParseFrame.ownChildren`, `FRUSDocumentParser.swift`): a section that holds documents and prints text of its own is given a row under its own `xml:id`, holding its heading and what is written directly inside it, and none of what its documents hold. Its kind need not be one the index promotes as prose: the 107 meetings of `frus1952-54v05p1` and `p2` are `subsection`s. A heading alone, a footnote on the heading and an empty paragraph are not text of its own; an image is. A list (persons, sources, a table of contents, an index) and a section with no `xml:id` are never rows (`decidedKind(of:)`, the one rule both parses ask).
- **Its page breaks.** A break is part of the row only when text of the section's own follows it before the next division inside it. One followed by a document is the page that document begins on, as before. Each division's place among its parent's children is recorded in one statement as it closes (`ParseFrame.childDivisionRanges`), so a section's own text is what lies outside those places.
- **The reader's page is the row.** A parse for one section (`parseDocument`, `parseDocumentWindow`) makes the index's decisions from the section's opening tag, so the reader opens the nodes the whole volume's parse emits. Until now it decided nothing inside the section. A section the index leaves out has no row to agree with and still opens whole, without its documents, by a second reading of the file (`parseTarget`).
- **The index** (`IndexingPipeline.swift`): `currentDateIndexVersion` 67 → 68. The row is stored as a promoted section's is: no start page, its own breaks, its cross-references, people and source note collected, `is_front_matter` by its kind. `mergeReadingSequence` puts a section's own row first in the section; it was appended after everything else in the volume.
- **Browse** (`VolumeSection.ownTextEntry(among:)`, `BrowserViewModel.compilationOwnText`, `CompilationView.ownTextSection`, the Mac's `CorpusSectionDocumentView`): the row is drawn first in the section, above its sections and documents, as **Read** and the section's title, with one new sentence under it: "The text this section prints outside the documents and sections it holds." Both platforms find the row by the one kit rule, in the index's rows they already load. It opens the index's own row.

**Found by the suites and by a first measurement, and changed**
- *The first build's rows held text from divisions inside the section*: a table of contents, a persons list, the placeholders of chapters not yet released, eight editorial-note introductions (18 rows). A section's own text is now what is written directly inside it.
- *The first build kept every break but the last ones*, so a section whose breaks sit between its documents (324 of the rows) claimed every page from its first break to its last: 114 pages in six volumes named a section beside the document printed there. The rule above is the fix.
- *`ContainerTests`' "Opening a left-out container by id still renders everything it holds"* failed on the first build, which gave such a section its heading alone. The second reading is the fix.
- *Comparing two node trees by `"\(nodes)"` reported nine sections that differ.* An element's attributes are a dictionary, and two equal dictionaries can print in different orders. The comparison now sorts them, in the corpus check and in the committed test.

**Measured.** Two full indexes of the 553 catalogue volumes at corpus `99d851c79` were built through the kit's own `IndexingPipeline` (`indexAllVolumes`, then the post-index passes) in a throwaway package test, one from `v2` @ `af64ceae` at version 67 and one from this branch, about 7 minutes each, and compared by SQL. The whole-volume parse was also dumped row by row at both revisions and at the final commit, whose dump is byte for byte the one the second index was built from. Nothing here was committed.
- **Rows:** 316,814 → 318,151. **1,337 added in 139 volumes, none removed, none changed** in header, dateline, source note, text or flags, and the rows both hold are in the same order. The 1,337 are the 1,332 the brief counted from the XML and five whose own content is an image and no words (`frus1902app1` `ch6`, `frus1919Parisv01` `ch2`, `frus1941-43` `ch6`, `frus1943` `ch3subch13`, `frus1969-76ve05p2` `ch3`).
- **Their text:** 1,421,459 characters, median 351; 95 rows under 100 characters, 160 of 1,000 or more, 22 of 10,000 or more, the longest 86,036 (`frus1872p2v1` `comp3`). 14 are front matter by their kind, all in `frus1902app1`. The conference volumes hold most of them: `frus1941-43` 143, `frus1943` 126, `frus1945Berlinv02` 113, `frus1952-54v05p2` 71, `frus1943CairoTehran` 70, `frus1945Malta` 54, `frus1944Quebec` 42, `frus1952-54v05p1` 36.
- **Page rows:** 318 added, all for the new rows and none a start; 106 of the rows have one. No existing page row changed.
- **Citation Lookup's page answers**, by `PageSpanResolver`'s rule replayed over both indexes' page rows: of 504,863 pages that name something in either, **208 in 20 volumes named nothing and now name a section**; in `frus1969-76ve05p2`, which numbers its pages in every document, page 1 gains a section among the 158 documents that share the number; no other answer changes, and no volume's per-document verdict.
- **Stored page references:** two change, `frus1919Parisv01` Documents 58 and 61, whose "See diagram on page 112." was left unresolved and is now an edge to `ch2`, the section that prints the diagram. None moves from a document to a section.
- **Cross-references:** 185,529 → 187,318. 1,789 are from 316 of the sections: 1,344 inside their volume, 445 into another (383 to a document, 62 to a whole volume). One is marked broken, by the bundled index, which is read by volume and target.
- **People:** 612,104 → 616,565 mentions. The 4,461 are in 358 of the sections (`frus1945Berlinv02` 1,245, `frus1943CairoTehran` 1,012, `frus1945Malta` 911, `frus1952-54v05p2` 809, `frus1952-54v05p1` 345). 96 people, counted by volume, had no mention and now have one. Brigadier General Esposito is named in the list of those present at seven of the Joint Chiefs' meetings at Potsdam and in none of their minutes: no mention in `frus1945Berlinv02` at version 67, seven at 68.
- **Dates and sources:** 110 of the rows are dated, by a date their own text prints; 86 are meetings of `frus1952-54v05p1` and `p2`. 15 have a source note (8 a decimal file number, 2 a named file, 5 no archival citation). 33 footnote citations in 3 sections are stored as external citations.
- **The reader's page:** for every one of the 3,535 rows that are sections, the parse for that one section gives the nodes of its row, and none has no page. Run at the final commit.
- **Not in the corpus:** a list that holds a document, a division that holds a transparent wrapper holding a division, and a legacy `editorialNote` div. Counted over the 553 files.

**Tests**
- `SectionOwnTextTests` (`FRUSExplorerTests/FRUSCoreKit/IndexingPipelineTests.swift`, 17 tests, in the package and in Xcode): one fixture volume in which each section is there for one rule, followed from the file to the parse, to the index through the pipeline's own store pass (rows, Search, flags, references, page rows and `PageRangeStore`'s answers), to the reader's page for every row, to the reading order and to Browse's rule.

The Mac's loader cannot be run by a test target, so its call of the kit rule and both views' order are held by their source.
- **Each rule removed in turn**, with the test that failed named: twenty in the kit, run in a second worktree (every section given a row; an image not counted; a heading counted; a stretch keeping its closing breaks, and the last stretch; a division's text counted as the section's; no division's place recorded; a left-out section not read again, and decided again on the second reading; a parse for one section deciding nothing; a list decided; a section with no id decided; the front-matter flag dropped; a section that holds documents passed up as one that holds a promoted section; the reading order not putting the row first, and making up a page for a section without one; the version left at 67; a made-up id naming a row; a leaf given a row; the first row returned) and four in the app (the loader not keeping the row; the iPhone's view drawing it below the sections; the Mac not looking for it; the Mac finding it by a rule of its own). ## Session 2026-10-11 — Two Browse UI tests are released by the test and not by a clock, a test's process starts no Live Activity, and #1577 lane 2's last Mac check is made

Asked for by the owner when #1640 merged, before pull request D of the index bump: find and resolve the two `BrowseNestedSectionTests` failures of pull request C's run, and download the search model into the Mac check copy for the one check of #1577's lane 2 that was still owed. No index version, no CloudKit deploy, no `@Model` or stored property, no string a reader meets, no shared code. The app changes are DEBUG-only seams and one rule about Live Activities that holds in a test's process alone.

**The two failures were two different things, and the iPad leg added two more.**

**1. Each test held a seam back for a number of seconds counted from launch.** `testAPipelineArrivingLateFillsTheOpenCompilation` asked for the pipeline 25 seconds after launch (`FRUS_UI_TEST_DELAY_PIPELINE`) and first required the "Search Index Unavailable" banner; `testAnIndexStartedElsewhereFillsTheOpenCompilation` asked for the seeded volume's download to finish 30 seconds after launch (`FRUS_UI_TEST_FINISH_SEEDED_DOWNLOAD_AFTER`) and first required "Index Required". On iPhone 17 (iOS 27.0) that afternoon the walk from launch to the compilation took 46 to 50 seconds, each XCUI query 2 to 3.5 seconds, so the pipeline had attached and the volume was indexed before either test looked. Each failed on its own check of its premise, and each failed the same way on `v2` @ `af64ceae`, built in a second worktree. An iPhone under iOS 26.5 spent about as long on each step, so it is not iOS 27's; why the walk is slower than when the tests were written was not found.
- **The seams now wait for the test.** `FRUS_UI_TEST_HOLD_PIPELINE=1` and `FRUS_UI_TEST_FINISH_SEEDED_DOWNLOAD_ON_SIGNAL=1` hold each seam until a Darwin notification arrives (`UITestBrowseSeams.onSignal`, `notify_register_dispatch` on the main queue, the registration cancelled at its first delivery), and each test posts its signal (`notify_post`) once it has seen the screen its premise names. A Darwin notification crosses from the runner to the app in one simulator. The two delay keys are gone.
- `BrowseSeamSignalTests` (unit target, 2): an action runs on its own signal, once, and not on the other's; and the UI suite's source arms each key and sends the name the app listens for, after an assertion.

**2. "Could not reach the 'Browse' tab" on a run's first test was the app opening on its onboarding wizard**, twice that afternoon by chance, once before any change here was made. The process on screen had none of the test's launch arguments and none of its environment. Read from the simulator's log:
- **The system opens the app in the background when one of its Live Activities is dismissed while the app is not running.** A test's app is seldom running by then: a UI test that taps Index Now passes once the rows are drawn and its app is killed while it indexes, and a unit run that takes a second ends while its host indexes a volume it found at launch. The activity has nothing to end it, the next `xcodebuild` run's install stops it (`liveactivitiesd`: "Stopping uninstalled activity"), and the request to open the app follows.
- **A launch a test asks for while that background launch is starting is given its process.** SpringBoard logs "Bootstrapping … with intent background" and "Initial launch state: BG-Active" where a test's launch reads `foreground-interactive` and `FV-Focal`.
- **Counted:** four installs stopped an activity left over, two by chance and two made on purpose, and the launch after each came up in the background and showed the wizard, the test's request 9 to 23 ms behind `liveactivitiesd`'s. No other launch did: of the 20 the log holds up to the third, after 11 installs, the other 17 came up in front. Each of the four tests failed in 12 to 15 seconds.
- **An activity the app does end brings the same request**, when its dismissal comes due three seconds later and the process has gone: 3.013 seconds after the end, twice out of two. Neither met a test's launch.

**What was built for it**
- **A test's process starts no Live Activity** (`LiveActivityPolicy.mayShow(in:)`, at the end of `AppState.swift`): not a unit test's host (`XCTestConfigurationFilePath`) and not a UI test's app (`FRUS_UI_TEST_MODE`). Both of the app's requests, for indexing and for summarizing, ask it first. A reader's app is unchanged.
- **`TabBarNavigator` names the cause** when a selection fails over the wizard, for the two cases the rule cannot reach: the tests of a build older than the rule, and the app killed by hand while it indexes.
- `LiveActivityPolicyTests` (unit target, 3): the rule's fixtures, one for each conjunct; the app's own indexing progress path driven in the test host with a real pipeline, where no activity may appear and a progress update must have been handled; and a census of every request for an activity in the app's source, each behind the rule.

**3. And the iPad leg found a third thing: the walk took whichever subseries came first.** The suite launches with downloaded volumes only and tapped the first row labelled "Subseries". The UI-test app shares a simulator's volumes with every other run on it, and the iPad Pro 13-inch (M5) under iOS 27.0 holds `frus1964-68v01` and `v02` from other work: the first match there was "Subseries 1964-68, 35 volumes", and the suite's first test failed one step on, with "The seeded volume's row did not appear in the subseries list". An iPhone 17 under iOS 26.5 that held another session's volumes had failed with the same message earlier in the day, and was then read as that simulator's state and left.
- **The walk opens the fixture's own subseries, by name** ("Subseries 1961-63"). The simulator's volumes were not touched.
- The same test on the same iPad failed before the change (70.6 seconds) and passed with it (125.7 seconds).
- `UIObstructionTests`, `TwoPaneDocumentTests`, `AuxWindowCloseTests` and `CompilationDocumentsTests` still take the first subseries row. (Since A12, #1694, 2026-10-20, every walk among them that goes on to the fixture volume names its subseries; the three queries that read nothing inside the row keep the first.)

**4. And one read made at once, where it should wait.** In the suite's run on that iPad, `testLevelStateSurvivesBackInTwoPane` typed "Bator Papers" into Archives' search, read the field in the next statement and got "Bator Pape" (`typeSearch`'s precondition). The session was building an index on the same Mac at that moment.

**Measured, before and after, on iPhone 17 (iOS 27.0)**
- *Before the rule:* `testIndexingFromTheCompilationFillsItsDocumentList`, run by itself, passed and left an activity nothing had ended; the cold-volume test, run next as the first of a new run, opened on the wizard and failed in 11.8 seconds.

Run again, it passed.

**The last Mac check of #1577's lane 2** (pull request #1633 left it for a copy with the search model: with a keyword search on screen, Facets while a Meaning search runs should describe the keyword rows, in the keyword wording, until the Meaning list arrives).
- **The model was downloaded into the check copy with the owner's leave**, given twice: for the 229 MB download, and for the app's own sheet, which asks the reader to agree to the Gemma Terms of Use before it fetches Google's EmbeddingGemma. The copy holds `embeddinggemma-300m-qat-Q4_0.gguf`, 229,093,184 bytes, and 12 MB of match files the app then fetched by itself for the 32 volumes the copy has.

At the switch to Meaning, while the header read "Searching…" and the keyword rows were still on screen, the panel still read "Describing all 364 matches". When the Meaning list arrived, "14 closest matches", it read "Describing the 14 closest matches", over "Counted over the results themselves, not the whole corpus. Narrowing to a row returns exactly its documents."

**Checked**
- `build-for-testing` of the `FRUSExplorer` scheme (iPhone 17, iOS 27.0), over an existing build folder: `** TEST BUILD SUCCEEDED **`, and no warning line but the two known residues.
- **`BrowseNestedSectionTests` on iPhone 17 (iOS 27.0)**, the whole suite, 600 seconds a test: "Executed 11 tests, with 4 tests skipped and 0 failures", `** TEST EXECUTE SUCCEEDED **`. The two that had failed passed in 55.6 and 56.2 seconds. Every one of its seven launches came up in front, and the system created no Live Activity during it.

Both tests that had failed on the iPhone passed there (100.3 and 103.1 seconds), and all nine launches came up in front. **With the read waiting, that test by itself passed in 676.5 seconds.** Two runs before that one were ended at ten minutes while still walking: `-maximum-test-execution-time-allowance` does not raise the default, and the run that passed set `-default-test-execution-time-allowance 1500` as well.

- **The suites this changes and the tree's gates, by themselves**, before the full run and again on the tree as committed: 116 tests in 9 suites passed (the two new suites, the seeder's and the summary card's, `AppSourceTreeTests`, `EditableContentKeyTests`, `CodingStandardsAuditTests`, `FRUSCoreKitBoundaryTests`, `UnconstructedViewAuditTests`). No ranged block moved. The census had first walked the app's folder by itself, which `AppSourceTreeTests` refuses: found by reading that audit before any run, and the census reads through `AppSourceTree` now.
- **The iOS unit target** on iPhone 17 (iOS 27.0): "Test run with 7013 tests in 826 suites passed after 695.107 seconds with 6 known issues", `** TEST EXECUTE SUCCEEDED **`, exit 0, no failed line and no restart of the host. 5 tests and 2 suites more than pull request C's run; it ran beside the two Mac builds, which is its 695 seconds. **The system created no Live Activity during it.** Each of the two full runs made that afternoon before the rule created six.

## Session 2026-10-11 — Index version 69: a Subject-Numeric file stores its class key, with a subject number or without one, and one file has one list of neighbours

Pull request D of the index bump (`Planning/Index-Bump-Brief-2026-10-11.md`, §3.7; decision 5), begun after #1641 merged, in the session that wrote the brief and pull requests A, B and C. Index version 69, so every library re-indexes once at the build that carries the bump. No CloudKit deploy, no `@Model` or stored property, no table or column. Four bundled files are regenerated. No issue was filed for it: the owner asked for the pull request, and the text of an issue is offered in it.

**The defect.** `document_sources.decimal_class` is what Source Explorer's Archival Neighbors, Browse ▸ Archives and Archival Analytics know a central file by. Of the 9,443 documents that cite a Subject-Numeric file, 2,613 stored none, so each was in the Subject-Numeric File category and in no file: no neighbours, and no row in any list of files.

**Measured first**, as the brief asked. A full index of the 553 catalogue volumes at corpus `99d851c79` was built through the kit's own `IndexingPipeline` from `v2` at version 68, in a throwaway package test, and every one of its 264,635 stored source notes was read again through `SourceNoteKit`. The index and the kit agreed on the form of every note, and on the class of all but ten (below). The 2,613:
- **285 needed no new grammar.** `CollectionKeying.centralFilesReading`, #1543's rule that places a citation by its form, already read a class for them, and `IndexingPipeline.decimalClassColumn` stored none. For 173 the pipeline scanned a note parsed as a National Archives collection only when the parsed series named the central files, and `RG 59, Records of the Department of State, Central Files, 1967–69, PET 3 OECD` parses with the record group's own name as its series. For 112 the scan reads comma segments, and a classification follows the designation with no full stop (`Central Files, POL 26-1 S VIET Top Secret.`).
- **768 print a subject number in a spelling the class grammar refused:** a space beside a dash (`POL 32-1 INDIA- PAK`), a country word longer than six letters (`POL 3 MALAYSIA`), a post in parentheses (`DEF 18-3 USSR (MO)`), stops (`DEF 19–8 U.S.-IRAN`), an ampersand (`POL 19 RHOD & NYAS`), a dash joining the number to what stands beside it (`E–8 INDON`, `POL 7-Nigeria`), a commodity joined to its category (`INCO–GRAINS 4 UK -US`), or a country not in capitals (`POL 27 S Viet`).
- **1,498 print no subject number** (`POL US–USSR`, `AID (US) S VIET`, `INCO–GRAINS GATT`). The 1963 handbook's instructions for `POL` let an office file under the primary subject alone and arrange the papers by country ("POLITICAL AFFAIRS & REL, France"; for relations between countries, "India-Pakistan"), so these are files and not designations cut short. Neither handbook's text calls one a general file; the code calls it a primary-subject file.
- **62 are left without a class:** 7 give a block of years and nothing else, and 55 print what the app does not read as a designation (a handling caption, `POL Nodis`; prose run on after the number; a country that is no area code with no number before it, `POL Nigeria-US`; a designation with no category, `JAPAN–KOR S`).
- **The Archives Visit packet**, the brief's third change, was already done by #1543 (`TripPacketBuilder` takes the kit's designation).

**What was built**
- **One definition of the class a note stores** (`CollectionKeying.centralFilesClass(parsed:note:)`, `SourceNoteKit`). The pipeline stores what it returns, the neighbour route reads it again from the note, and the generators key by it. The pipeline's own copy of the gate had parted from the kit's: it read a series named `Central Decimal File 1910–1929` and the kit did not, so ten notes of `frus1917-72PubDip` stored a class the usage index never counted. The definition is the comma scan where the parse is central-files-shaped and, where that finds nothing, the class the form rule reads or the class of the designation it finds.
- **A designation read part by part** (`SourceNoteParser.SubjectNumericDesignation`): its lead, a commodity joined by a dash, an agency in parentheses, the subject number, the country element and a post. `decimalClassKey(_:)` falls back to it when the strict shape refuses a candidate, and respells what it reads as the strict shape spells one. It is looser about the country element than the strict shape, so it is stricter about the lead: a handbook category or an organization lead, and nothing else.
- **A country not in capitals** is read when every word in title case is a word of the handbooks' own area codes (`ParsedSourceNote.subjectNumericAreaWords`, 155 words, a copy of the bundled label table's `areas`, pinned to it by a test), and, in a document's own citation only, when one or two words follow a subject number (`POL 28 Berlin`, `POL 7 US Kennedy`).
- **A file with no subject number has a class** (`SourceNoteParser.primarySubjectClassKey(ofDesignation:)`), read only from a designation the form rule found behind a central-files anchor, never from a front-matter item or a footnote: its shape alone is a category and some capitals.
- **A dash between two countries is kept.** `collapsingClassPunctuation` removed the first dash a space followed, for the decimal suffix (`751G.5– MSP`); it now does so only when the word before the dash begins with a digit.
- **The fold** (`CollectionKeying.subjectNumericParts(of:)`, which `subjectNumericGroup` now returns the group of): a key with no number folds to its head, the category with its commodity and agency (`POL US-USSR` to `POL`, `AID (US) INDIA` to `AID (US)`), and a numbered key with a commodity to head and number (`INCO-WOOL 17`). No key of the version-68 vocabulary has either, so no existing group moves.
- **The family query** (`IndexingPipeline.classLeafPatterns`, `classFamilyExclusion`, `classFamilyClause`, shared by the neighbours list and its badge): a head with no number is a prefix of every numbered file of the subject, which `LIKE` cannot leave out, so its family is its patterns less a `GLOB`; and a file with a country is matched as itself, because its space branch could only reach another country's file.
- **The neighbour route** (`CollectionKeying.matchesOnClass`, first in `IndexingPipeline.relatedDocuments(for:)`): a National Archives collection with no lot and any class, and a Department-worded note with a Subject-Numeric class, are matched on the class. Until now the second was matched on its stored file number, which finds the documents that print the designation the same way and none that cite it through the National Archives.
- **Source Explorer** (`SourceExplorerView`, `MacSourceExplorerView`): the empty state, the "Matching archival source" line of both platforms and the line above the list on iPhone and iPad (`archivalNeighborBasis(for:…)`) all ask the route's own rule. The last read "Same collection — RG 59, Records of the Department of State" over a list that is now the file's.
- **The labels** (`SubjectNumericLabelTable`): a head with no number reads "Files with no subject number" (`archival.classLabel.noSubjectNumber`); a file with no number reads as its country and takes no organization's name before it; and a post is left off the country element before it is looked up. The label generator divides a key through the kit now.
- **The index** (`IndexingPipeline.swift`): `currentDateIndexVersion` 68 → 69.

**Found by the measurements, and changed**
- *The first authority regenerated from the branch keyed two subject titles as countries.* `frus1969-76ve08` lists two embassies' files by title under their lots, `DEF 18–4 Defense Affairs, Arms Control and Disarmament` and `SOC 14 Human Rights`, and "one or two words after a subject number" took the title for the country. That reading is now a document's own citation's alone, where its 23 words over 142 notes are all names; a front-matter item is read by the area-code rule and by the capitals rule.
- *The line above the neighbours list on iPhone and iPad was a second copy of the route's rule*, and was found only on reading the manual's sentence about it.
- *Two fixtures of the pipeline test were not the notes of the documents named beside them, and four notes in new tests were constructed and not marked so.* Every fixture note in the tests this pull request adds or changes was then checked against the stored notes, and each document named beside one against what that document stores.
- *The term.* The first draft of the code and of these notes called a file with no subject number a general file. Neither handbook's text layer has the phrase, and the label table's own comments use it for something else.
- *The unit run found the Archives Visit keys* (below): `TripPacketBuilderTests` and `ArchiveVisitKeyStabilityTests` each pinned a key the change moved.
- *The iPhone's class list showed a row this change added reading a piece of another line.* `AID (US) INDIA` read "programs in Spanish speaking countries). Aeronautics — India": under 1964–1973 `AID` is read through the organization branch, whose name for it is broken in the table (below). A file with no number now takes no organization's name, which is what the code's own comment had said it did. `AID` is the one category that reached that branch with such a file: 22 keys over 52 documents.

**Measured, version 68 against version 69.** Two full indexes, the second built from this branch, compared table by table (`document_sources`, `volume_sources` and `external_citations` column by column; every other table by a digest of its rows, with surrogate ids and the version stamp left out).
- **`document_sources`:** 2,593 rows gain a class (2,551 Subject-Numeric, 40 decimal numbers worded `RG 59, Records of the Department of State, Decimal File 1945–49`, 2 whose second sentence cites a file); 178 change it, each to get back a dash; **none loses one**; no row changes its form. `series_name` changes in 77 rows, the Department-worded notes whose stored file number had lost the same dash. 9,381 of the 9,443 Subject-Numeric rows have a class, on 1,929 distinct keys (6,830 on 1,361).
- **`volume_sources`:** 172 rows in 46 volumes gain a class, each a file designation with a subject number in the volume's list of sources that the strict shape refused (`DEF 18-3 USSR (MO): …`, `POL 27 Laos: military operations`), and one changes (`frus1961-63v18`, a row that lists three designations, the first of which is now read). 3,207 rows in 108 volumes store a Subject-Numeric class.
- **`external_citations`: identical.** So are the documents, the text index's vocabulary, dates, cross-references, people, pages and subjects.
- **Files with no subject number:** 303 keys over 1,498 documents, 127 of them with one document; 30 heads, of which `POL` has 1,242.
- **Both wordings:** 271 files are cited through the Department and through the National Archives, by 2,180 documents in the first wording and 2,499 in the second.

**The bundled files.** A control was built first: the generators at `v2` (`76db1e09`), run over the same corpus at each shipped file's own stamp. Eight files came out byte for byte as shipped, so each difference on the branch is this pull request's.
- **`collection-authority.json`** (and its report): 4,051 → 3,985 records. 66 ids go and none is added: Sources rows that are a file designation, 62 of them with its description (`INCO–WOOL 17 US–JAPAN: Wool trade between the U.S. and Japan`; 25 from `frus1964-68v09`, 20 from `frus1969-76ve13`), each of which had been a collection named by its own text. 19 records change in their children. The three era blocks lose children that were designations with no subject number read from document notes (`POL CUBA.`): they are class children now, which ship only where front matter cites them.
- **`collection-usage-index.json`:** 11,027 class keys (10,455); 193,068 notes with a class (190,465); 76,131 in a collection (75,045). The Central Files record holds 18,689 documents in 119 volumes (17,613 in 118), and the authority lists 158 volumes for it (157).
- **`provenance-flow-index.json`** and **`external-citation-index.json`** follow the authority. What footnotes point at is unchanged.
- **Unmoved:** `volume-sources-index.json`, `source-provenance-index.json`, `series-facts-index.json`, `lot-claimants-index.json`.

## Session 2026-10-12 — The iPhone's language-analysis record is read, and the printed-form fallback for Collocates becomes a lane before build 50 (#1608)

After #1649 merged the owner asked how to get the Collocates record off the phone at once, without waiting for the Copy button of the small-fixes pull request, collected it, and decided on what it showed. Planning documents alone: no file the app, a kit, a generator or a test compiles is changed.

**How it was collected**
- Build 49 writes the record to the phone's system log at the default level (`NaturalLanguageReadiness.record`, unchanged since the `build-49` tag), so nothing had to be reproduced. The owner ran `sudo /usr/bin/log collect --device-name … --last 7d --predicate …` on the Mac with the phone attached, on 2026-10-11 at 23:47 EDT.
- **The predicate was not applied.** The archive was the phone's whole system log for the week: 2.4 GB, 86,383,244 events, every process. Read from it: the app's own process, and three minutes of the asset services' lines that name the linguistic data. The owner deleted the archive after the reading; the app process's extracts are in the session's notes.
- **The phone keeps the app's own lines for about nine hours.** They have no time-to-live and sit in the archive's `Persist` store, which held 51 files and 501 MB, the oldest closed at 15:03 that day. Lines the system's frameworks write with a time-to-live (`Special`) went back the whole week.

**What it holds**
- **The build.** All fourteen processes of the app in the week carry the binary UUID `790A33F4-D9A7-322C-8419-2976358CF52E`, the arm64 UUID of build 49's iOS archive on this Mac. The phone is on iOS 27.0.1.
- **One session's record**, a launch at 23:44: `warm-up started; trigger=firstForeground app=active age=2897.136s`, and 30 seconds later `verdict … assets LexicalClass=available@0.105s NameType=available@0.005s Lemma=timedOut@30.005s withheld=[Lemma]; canary lemmas=false classes=true names=true`. The first of #1608's three paths: iOS never answered the lemma request. The process was 48 minutes old and had written no line until the app was opened, which is what prewarming looks like.
- **iOS's own framework, in the app's process** (`com.apple.NaturalLanguageFramework`): the assets for lexical classes and for names "are available", inside a tenth of a second; then `Placing request with asset download service for 'Lemma', language: 'en'`, `Assets for 'Lemma' … are downloading` and `Adding 'Lemma' - 'en' to fulfillment queue`, and nothing more before the process's last line three minutes later. No line of `mobileassetd` in those minutes names a download of linguistic data.
- **Not in it:** how often it happens (the ten earlier processes that asked for the language assets that week have no verdict line left), a launch that worked, a re-check, and whether the "downloading" state ever ends. The asset frameworks' own lines for the earlier launches survive and show the same asset sources every time; the number of asset-set lookups in a launch's first minute differs (12 in six launches, 13 in one, 14 in three, tonight's among them, 41 in one), which may tell a good launch from a bad one and was not verified.

**Decided by the owner**
- **The printed-form fallback is a lane, before build 50.** It is the plan of record's decision 8 and pull request 3 of its queue, between the small fixes and the build. The condition the owner set on 2026-09-29 stands: each surface that falls back says so, says why, and says that results can differ from a device that reduces words to their dictionary forms.
- **The record is on the issue**, as the owner asked: #1608, comment of 2026-10-12.

**Docs**
- `Planning/Plan-Of-Record-2026-10-11.md`: decision 8 in §0; the queue renumbered in §1, with what the lane builds; §2's hold on the build and one more TestFlight line; §3 loses the record it was waiting for and gains the optional five-launch sample for a Feedback report to Apple; §4's item on the lemmatiser states the measurement.

**Checked**
- `CodingStandardsAuditTests` on iPhone 17 under iOS 27.0: 63 tests in 1 suite passed, `planOfRecordMatchesTheVisualMarketingPlan` among them. The two files it reads were as committed; the session's own entry was written after. No other test reads a file this change touches, so the full unit run, `swift test` and the Mac build were not run.

**Not done**
- No frequency: five launches in a row and a collection of the last hour would give it, and a good launch's framework lines beside a bad one's.
- No Feedback report to Apple.
- The Copy button stays in the small-fixes pull request, with a new reason: a tester has no other way to send lines the phone keeps for nine hours.

## Session 2026-10-12 — The Subject-Numeric label table is read from the handbooks' own text layer, comes out the same on every system tried, and is regenerated with its wrong readings put right (#1644)

Pull request 1 of the queue in `Planning/Plan-Of-Record-2026-10-11.md` (§1), begun after #1649 and #1650 merged. One bundled file is regenerated, `subject-numeric-labels.json`. No index version (`currentDateIndexVersion` stays 69) and no re-index, by the owner's decision of 2026-10-11; no CloudKit deploy, no `@Model` or stored property, no table or column, no new or renamed resource. The handbooks stay local.

**The defect.** The shipped table read some files wrongly and build 49 shows it. Under 1964–1973 `UK` read *Ukraine*, `UAR` *United Arab Republic USCG US Coast Guard*, `USSR` *Union of Soviet Socialist* and `UN` *Universe*, and every numbered `AID` file read a piece of another line; under 1963 `CUBA` read *Council for U.S. Aid (Nationalist China)*, `IA` *Iran (Azerbaijan)* and `NR EAST` *Niger, Republic of and East Africa*; `FIN` read *Algerian National Liberation Front* under both. The table was a month behind the corpus's keys (index version 69 added the files with no subject number), its `coverage` block described an older usage index, and `SubjectNumericLabelGenerator` no longer wrote the shipped table from the same handbooks on macOS 27.0.1.

**Why the generator stopped reproducing its table: measured.** The generator at the commit that wrote the table (`33cbbddb`, 2026-09-08, on macOS 26.6.2), with that commit's inputs, was run in four places. Natively on macOS 27.0.1 it wrote 78 of the 1963 schedule's 1,897 labels respaced, `US` for `USIS` in the abbreviations, and 121 areas renamed. Inside the iOS 27.0 simulator runtime (`xcrun simctl spawn`, the environment passed as `SIMCTL_CHILD_*`) it wrote the same differences. Inside the iOS 26.5 runtime it wrote the shipped table but for seven entries at the footer's edge, where the two platforms place a line's top differently. So the operating system's text extraction changed between 26 and 27 and nothing else did: the generator took its lines from PDFKit (`selectionsByLine()`), and PDFKit decides for itself where a word ends. Fitted against iOS 26.5's own lines over every page, its rule was a space wherever the gap exceeds half a space of the earlier run's font (best threshold 0.500 in the 1963 handbook and 0.498 in the 1965 one; 238 disagreements in 71,193 pairs, and 3 in 1,290). OS 27 follows no rule over gaps: it joins `PROPER` and `TY` across 4.4 points and divides `US` from `IS` across 0.8.

**What was built**
- **The text layer is read from the content stream, and PDFKit is asked nothing** (`TextLayerReader`, `StandardFontMetrics`, `Handbook`; the Core target no longer imports PDFKit). Acrobat's Paper Capture wrote each recognised word as its own string at its own place, in eight of the standard fonts with no `/Widths` and one hidden composite font with a `ToUnicode` map. The 1963 layer puts no space in any string (94,170 of them) and the 1965 layer ends each word's string with one (90,262 of 91,989), so the layer says where nearly every word break is; where it wrote none, the half-space rule decides, on the fonts' own widths (Adobe's metrics for the standard 14, for the 95 ASCII codes and the seven above them the handbooks use). A page that uses anything the reader does not model (another font, a rotated or skewed matrix, text rise, a form XObject, a code with no width) throws.
- **A line is the runs that follow one another in the stream**, each to the right of the last and on its baseline (within a quarter of the smaller type size), cut where a gap exceeds twice the smaller type size. The stream's order is used for that and nothing else: the 1965 outlines set two columns within 13 points of one another on one baseline, and only the capture's own lines keep them apart. The rows of a table are still put together by height. Checked against PDFKit on macOS 27, where the two can be compared: all 22,093 lines of the 1963 handbook that the reader reproduces have their left and right edges where PDFKit puts them to four decimals, and all but one of the 17,866 of the 1965 one within a twentieth of a point.
- **The same table in every runtime tried.** The shipped file has SHA-256 `11d4c4d487fa92f8106cf36f71a927630a4797003f5fd4eade7bb2439a9f527a` written natively on macOS 27.0.1, inside the iOS 26.5 runtime and inside the iOS 27.0 runtime, and a second native run writes it again.
- **The capture's unread mark.** Acrobat set a word it was unsure of in its hidden font, with a tilde where a character would not resolve (`BUDG~T`). PDFKit returned those words for the 1965 handbook and dropped all 320 for the 1963 one, which is why `BUD 10` read *PRESIDENT'S*. Read from the stream they are all there, and the generator throws while any label holds a tilde, naming each one.
- **Page attribution.** An index page is known by its dotted leaders (at least 44 such lines on an index page of the 1963 handbook and 9 of the 1965 one; no other page has more than 2 and 1) and is given to no category by either pass: the 1965 scan reads the word `Index` on none of its 73 index pages, and that is where the shipped `POL 15-4` came by the reading *BG*. One edition's categories are lent to the other where the corpus cites them, which is how the 1964–1973 schedule gains outlines for `AID`, `PET`, `CON`, `EP` and `INT`: the 1965 scan carries no legible mark for `AID` on any page. The scan's `NCO` for `INCO`, on five of the eight pages of that outline that carry a mark, is corrected by hand.
- **The common abbreviations.** The appendix's first page reads `Corn. Abbrev.` in both scans and was outside the span read (no code under A or B in 1963, none before `CINCEUR` in 1965), which is how `AID` came to be named by a piece of a later entry. A column is where two or more code-shaped lines begin within four points; a section letter is furniture; an organization's name is its entry up to the gloss. 433 and 445 entries are read where 319 and 279 were, and the artifact carries the six the corpus cites as an organization file's prefix (`CENTO`, `NATO`, `OAS`, `OECD`, `SEATO`, `UN`) and no others: shipping the appendix whole shipped *FM — Prime Minister RCA*.
- **The country element is read from the Department's printed list first.** The 1963 handbook calls its appendix "a list of standard country abbreviations … for use in coding papers relating to specific countries", and the 1965 edition says the list was "eliminated but can be obtained from the Division of Records Management, upon request". So one list governs both schedules: 235 codes, each named by the code-first table's own row less its parenthesis, checked against the name-first table and the decimal schedules' verified names, and looked up by its tokens in any order (`S VIET` is printed, `VIET S` is written). `AreaResolver` reads the curated readings, then the printed code, then the common abbreviations, then NARA's generative forms over the names. The abbreviations used to come first, which is how two misread codes outranked Finland and Cuba.
- **The coverage block** names the usage index it was counted against (`measuredAgainst`) and counts the areas as well as the subjects. `REVIEW_OUTPUT` writes every label with the page and row it was read from, which is the only way back to a scan that stays local.
- **The grammar's own lists** (decision 1). `ParsedSourceNote.subjectNumericAreaWords` is untouched, 155 words, and `DepartmentSeriesTests`' pin of it to the label table is replaced by `SubjectNumericGrammarListPinTests.theCountryWords`, which holds the 155 words literally. The same suite's pin of `subjectNumericCategories` to the table's category keys is replaced the same way (60 leads): the regenerated table names `SOCIO` where the list has `ORA`, so that pin would have failed too, and the reasoning is the decision's own. The table now holds 183 area-code words, 33 of them not in the grammar's list (`SWITZ`, `NETH`, `AUSTL`, `ALGERIA` among them) and 5 of the list's not in the table (`COAS`, `D`, `EA`, `FAA`, `IA`).
- **In the app:** one expectation of `PrimarySubjectFileLabelTests` (`POL GER W-US` reads *West Germany and United States*, the handbook's own name) and comments in `SubjectNumericLabelStore` and `SourceNoteParser`, each edit line for line so that no `Docs/EditableContent` range moves.

**The table, old against new**
- **Subjects.** 1963: 1,897 → 1,902 designators (23 changed, 5 added, none removed). 1964–1973: 1,648 → 1,777 (24 changed, 164 added, 35 removed), in 48 outlines where there were 44 (`NCO` gone; `AID`, `CON`, `EP`, `INT`, `PET` gained).

## Session 2026-10-12 — With no lemmatiser, Collocates, Distinctive sizing and Related Documents' shared words compare printed forms with a second corpus reference, and say so (#1608)

Pull request #1653, the third of the plan of record's queue, decision 8. It went ahead of pull request 2 (the small fixes, not yet opened) on the owner's word of 2026-10-12, since it depends on neither 1 nor 2; pull request 1 had merged (#1651, #1652). No index version and no CloudKit schema change.

**The ground**
- On build 49, in the foreground, under iOS 27.0.1, the owner's iPhone logged `Lemma=timedOut@30.005s withheld=[Lemma]; canary lemmas=false classes=true names=true`. iOS never answered the request for the English lemma data, and no change to the app's check can fix that.
- On such a launch Collocates refused, the word cloud's Distinctive sizing and Related Documents' shared-word chips were withheld, and the clouds said "Counted as printed". The corpus reference all three compare with, `keyness-baseline.json`, is counted in dictionary forms.

**What "printed" is, and one sentence of the brief that was wrong**
- The brief and the plan said the fallback "counts "missile" and "missiles" apart". Under the default settings it does not. The sentence comes from the 2026-09-28 plan's description of the option, written before anything was built.
- A printed count is the count a launch with no lemmatiser has made since #1373: the word's surface, lowercased, and then its regular plural folded by rule while *Merge plural and singular forms* is on (`WordCloudTokenizer.singularize`). The fallback keeps that count unchanged and gives it a reference counted the same way, which is what makes the comparison exact.
- So "missiles" is counted under "missile" in both references (34,909 in each), while "negotiate", "negotiated" and "negotiating" are three words (19,472, 9,272 and 15,267, against 44,011 for the dictionary form), "men" is not "man", and a name ending in s is clipped on both sides: "Dulles" is counted as `dulle` (32,456; the dictionary form `dulles` is 32,455). A chip shows the word as the page prints it.
- Every example in the new copy is therefore the verb pair. A plural would be a false example, and the shipped CSV caveat gave one (below).
- Counting plurals apart is another rule on both sides and a regeneration. It is the owner's to ask for; the plan's §3 has it.

**One value from the verdict to the count and to the reference**
- `WordCloudWordForm` (`.dictionary`, `.printed`), new in `WordCloudKit`. `NaturalLanguageHealth.wordForm` is `.printed` exactly when the verdict has no lemmatiser.
- A tokenizer told `.printed` asks the gate for `.tokenType` and no lemma scheme (`WordCloudTokenizer.wordSchemes`, `WordCloudMultiLensTokenizer.schemes`), so a lemmatiser that starts to answer part way through a count cannot mix the two forms in it. The default is `.dictionary`, and a tokenizer built without the argument counts as it did.
- `WordCloudTokenizer.configured(…wordForm:)`, the app's factory, takes the form with no default. Its four callers: the cloud's count and the collection export's cloud (the verdict's form), the Collocates configuration (the verdict's form) and the settings bench (`.dictionary`: it reads no tagger).
- `BundledKeynessBaseline` loads a file for each form and `baseline(for:tuning:includeDiplomatic:languageAnalysis:)` reads the one the verdict counts in. It returns a `KeynessReference` (terms, total, cut-off, form, distinct terms, stamp), which replaces the three-part tuple and the separate `coverage(for:)` and `generated`: a surface that says what it ranked against can no longer read those from the other file.
- A file is kept only under the form its own stamp names (`isReference(_:for:)`), in the bundle and in the test seam alike. `BundledArtifactProvenance` has a row for the new file.
- `prepare()` now waits for a load in flight. Before, a second caller returned at once and a read taken straight after was `.noArtifact` for a file a few milliseconds from being there; Related Documents awaits it before its lookup now.
- *Language analysis unavailable* is still returned in two cases: a part-of-speech lens counted without lexical classes, which counted nothing; and a launch with no lemmatiser whose printed-form file did not load. Both refusal sentences keep their text.

**The three surfaces**
- **Collocates.** `CollocationConfiguration` holds the verdict; its tokenizer counts in that verdict's form and both hosts (`SearchView`, the Mac's `SearchSheet`) read the reference for `configuration.languageAnalysis`, so one awaited verdict decides both. `CollocationAnalysis.rank` takes the form the neighbours were counted in and refuses a reference of the other form before it says anything about the query. A ranking of printed forms opens with a note as the list's first row. The two refusals that are results of the count, "No word appears at least 3 times…" and "Nothing near your matches is used more here…", carry the form too and are drawn under the same row, in a list that scrolls: counted as printed, "negotiated" twice and "negotiating" twice are two words under the floor, where a device that reduces words ranks "negotiate" at four.
- **Distinctive sizing.** `WordFrequencyService` counts a cloud in the form of the verdict it stamps the result with; `KeynessCloud.rank` already took the result's own stamp, and now ranks a result counted as printed against the printed reference and says which form in `Ranking.wordForm`. The header prints *Counted and compared as printed* under Distinctive and *Counted as printed* under Frequency, through `PrintedFormsNote`, which shows the line whole and puts it in a 96-point scrolling strip where the column has no room (seen at the largest accessibility size).
- **Related Documents' shared words.** `SemanticSharedTerms.sharedTerms` reads the reference for the verdict and hands it to `evidence(anchor:candidates:pipeline:reference:)`, which counts both documents in the reference's form and returns the form with the terms. The panel prints a note above its rows whenever their shared words were compared as printed, whether or not a row got a chip: with none, every row shows a percentage where a device that reduces words can name the words, and the note is what says why. The list reloads when the form the verdict counts in changes (`SemanticSharedTerms.reloadToken(for:)`), so "right now" stays true, and at no other re-check.
- A launch whose lemmatiser works takes none of these branches, and a Mac shows nothing new unless its own lemmatiser is missing: the fallback follows the verdict, not the platform.

**What each surface says** (the owner's condition of 2026-09-29: that it fell back and why, on screen, and that another device can differ)
- Six new strings, each with a block: `search.collocation.printedForms.note`; `wordcloud.keyness.comparedAsPrinted`; `related.sharedTerms.printedForms.note`; and for a Distinctive export `wordcloud.export.caveat.keyness.comparedAsPrinted` (the CSV), `wordcloud.export.caption.comparedAsPrinted` (the image's caption) and `wordcloud.export.axis.keyness.printed` (the axis label). Collocates and Related Documents have no export.
- The three on-screen sentences and the CSV's caveat say all three things, and `PrintedFormWordingTests` holds eight texts to them. The image caption's segment and the axis label are short labels on a line of labels: they say that the words were counted and compared as printed, as a cloud counted as printed has said in its caption since #1373.
- Two changed. `wordcloud.countedAsPrinted` gains "Counts can differ on a device that does: a Mac, or another iPhone or iPad." and is no longer cut at two lines. `wordcloud.export.caveat.countedAsPrinted` gave "negotiation" and "negotiations" as two words, which is false with plural folding on; it gives the verb pair.
- The Collocates note first closed with a sentence on the re-check. On an iPhone 17 it was then seven lines and left two rows of the ranking on screen, so the sentence went; the panel still rebuilds when a re-check adopts a lemmatiser.

**The reference**
- `keyness-baseline-printed.json`, 1,238,773 bytes (about 439 KB deflated). `keyness-baseline.json` gains `"wordForm":"dictionary"`, 24 bytes. Each app's bundle grows by 1,238,797 bytes.
- It comes out of the tagging pass that writes the first: `WordCloudMultiLensTokenizer.accumulate(from:into:printedInto:)` counts both forms of each token, each through the markings, the length and stopword test and the lens's filter by itself. `CloudVectorsAggregator.pack` takes the printed tally and stamps each baseline with its form.
- **The control came first.** The generator at `7c9eaacd`, unchanged, reproduced the three shipped files byte for byte from corpus `99d851c79` under their stamp of 2026-10-10: 20 minutes 7 seconds.
- **Then the changed generator.** Its `cloud-vectors-core.json` and `cloud-vectors-volumes.json` are the shipped ones apart from the date stamp, and its `keyness-baseline.json` apart from the stamp and the new key.
- **`VERIFY_PRINTED_WALK=1`** tokenises every document again as a device with no lemmatiser does, and throws before any write if a volume's tallies differ in any lens. A device builds two taggers for that count, one that also holds the lexical classes (Topics, Actions, Descriptors) and one that holds the token type alone (All terms, Concepts, Sentiment), so the run makes both walks. All 553 volumes, 314,616 documents, both taggers: no difference in any lens, and the four files the run then wrote are the committed ones byte for byte (the generator at `ddab192c`; 3,132 s of processor time against a plain run's 1,278). The one pass rests on two behaviours of a closed framework (a walk by `.lemma` and one by `.tokenType` find the same words; a word's lexical class does not depend on the lemma scheme being held), and this is their measurement.
- Measured on the file: All terms prices 97.61% of token mass (20,015 of 263,934 distinct, cut at 147) and Topics 97.88% (20,124 of 224,016, cut at 67); Actions 23,957 of 37,553 and Descriptors 22,877 of 39,295, both cut at 2; Concepts 166 and Sentiment 198, whole.
- **Memory.** The run had no autorelease pool, so nothing the tagger autoreleased was freed before the end: 24.93 GB of footprint for the unchanged generator and 49.05 GB with the first verify walk, on a Mac with 32 GB. Each document is now tokenised inside a pool, and a run peaks at 893 MB.
- **Time, on the M5 MacBook.** 21 minutes 24 seconds for a run (1,283.80 s; the unchanged generator took 1,206.79), and about 31 minutes more of processor time for the two verify walks. The plan's "50 to 60 minutes" was measured on another Mac in August.
- The run refuses (`printedReferenceIncomplete`) when a lens the first reference prices has no printed count.

## Session 2026-10-12 — Small fixes: the Archival Network and Browse ▸ Archives say one, Archival Neighbors list a volume by document number, a categorical Audio Graph gives each point its category, and the language-analysis record can be copied (#1643, #1617, #1608)

Pull request #1654, the second of the plan of record's queue. Pull request 1 had merged (#1651, #1652). Pull request 3 (#1653) went ahead of this one on the owner's word and closed #1608, so this one names #1608 and closes nothing of it. No index version and no CloudKit schema change.

**#1643 (a) and (b): a form for one**
- The Archival Network's dock set three counts in `%lld`, so with one of anything it read "1 collections share two or more volumes with this one", "1 more are held back" and "The 1 squares are central-file classes". The issue names the third; the other two sit beside it in `dockSummary` and had the same gap.
- Each is now a pair in `ArchivalCounts` (`networkPartners`, `networkHeldBack`, `networkClassSquares`), through `CountCopy.phrase`, with the count grouped. Between a pair only the words that agree with the count differ: "collection shares" and "collections share", "is" and "are", "square is a central-file class … while it is shown" and "squares are central-file classes … while they are shown".
- Browse ▸ Archives ▸ Classes labelled a class that one document cites "1 docs", and a volume in either drill list read "1 docs · 3%". The provenance doors' own row, which the issue also names, has been `CountCopy`'s since #1374. The class row is `CountCopy.docs`. Both drills (`ArchivesAxis.spec(forCategory:usage:)`, `ArchivesClassAxis.spec(for:era:usage:)`) had their own copy of the two accessory strings, by interpolation; they ask one function now, `ArchivesAxis.volumeAccessory(documents:sourcedDocuments:locale:)`, whose count is `CountCopy.docs` and whose one new string joins it to the share (`browser.archives.accessory.share %@ %@`, "%1$@ · %2$@%%").
- The count scan (`CodingStandardsAuditTests.countsGoThroughCountCopy`): six baseline entries gone, and the ceiling 286 → 280. `CountCopyWiringTests.sites` gains the six call sites.

**#1643 (c): Archival Neighbors, and where the order is made**
- Nine queries of `IndexingPipeline` ended `ORDER BY ds.volume_id, ds.document_id`, and an id is text: "Archival Neighbors – Central files POL" listed 1961–1963, vol. III as 126, 196, 198, 199, 218, 219, 233, 235, 292, 73, 86.
- **The order is made in the query**, in all nine, and not where the list is drawn. Each query cuts its rows with a `LIMIT` by the same order, so text order also chose which documents a long list showed: a volume's d1, d10, d100, d101. A sort in the view would put that selection in order and leave it the same selection. And a document's own sheet reads through `.stratified`, whose rows are the query's rows too: an order made for `.alphabetical` alone would have fixed the class list the issue was filed from and left Source Explorer's own list as it was.
- **`RelatedPoolOrdering` (#645) was read first.** Its two cases are about volumes: which of them a cut reaches. No case and no caller changes. `.stratified` still reads its whole container and takes one document from each volume in turn, so it reaches the volumes it reached and takes as many from each. Which of a volume's documents it takes follows the new order: the lowest-numbered first, where it took the first in text order. **So for a container larger than the pool, Related Documents' archival candidates from a volume are other documents of the same container than they were.** Every archival candidate has the same strength, 1.0, so what changes is which documents are in the pool, not how the archival axis scores one.
- `IndexingPipeline.relatedDocumentOrderSQL` is the one fragment the nine end with: the volume's id; the id's letters before its first number, as text; that number, as a number; the letters after it; a second number; and the id itself. Plain SQL (`LTRIM`, `SUBSTR`, `CAST`), so there is no collation to register on every connection that reads the index.
- It is number order and not the order the volume prints its documents in, which no column holds. A row's `rowid` was considered and left: `document_cache` is written by upsert, so a row's place is the history of one device.
- **Measured** over a full index (553 volumes, index v65, built 2026-10-08 on the iPhone 17e simulator, opened read-only). 264,575 source-note rows in 502 volumes. 263,999 of them, in 501 volumes, are `d`-numbered: number order puts none out of place against the order the volume was written in, where text order had 262,210 out of place in 483 volumes. The other 576, in twelve volumes, stand where text order put them beside the documents: 536 in `frus1958-60v05mSupp`, whose ids carry a country prefix (`bl_d1`) and now list each section by number; 39 appendix rows in ten volumes, before the documents; and one front-matter message in `frus1932v01`, after them. All 316,768 ids of `document_cache` are ASCII letters, digits, `_` and `-`; none starts with a digit; none has a third number; 120 have two, all `d710a-N` in `frus1945Berlinv02`.
- **Cost**, timed with the `sqlite3` shell on that index on the M5 MacBook, after the `COUNT(*)` each query runs first. A query whose rows came off the table's key in this order could stop at its limit and now reads every match and sorts: Nixon's NSC Files (7,069 rows, the largest container) 49 ms where it took 3; the Johnson National Security File (3,911) 40 where it took 31; the `POL` class family (4,556) 41 where it took 32; decimal file 893.00 (4,470, always read whole) 27 where it took 16; lot 54 D 270 (1,063), which sorted before, 3 where it took under 1.

**#1617: a point on a categorical axis is given its category**
- `AXAudiograph.h`: a data point's x value "should be a Double for a numeric x-axis or a String for a categorical x-axis", and of the value "only the `category` property will be used for data points in a categorical axis". Both builders of `AXChartDescriptorBuilder` declared a categorical axis from the points' labels and then gave each point a number, its position in the list (`firstIndex(of:)`, which is also one number for two equal points). So the one property the framework reads on that axis was empty for every bar of every ranking chart.
- One helper, `dataPoint(_:onNumericAxis:)`, makes every point for both builders: its number on a numeric axis, and its label, which is the name the axis lists, on a categorical one. A numeric axis is unchanged.
- **One label is one category**, which the review found the first version had not followed through. A name for an x value makes two points of one series under one label one category, where their positions were two. The header asks the axis for "every possible category value", so the single-series builder now lists a label once (`categories(of:)`; it listed it once for every point). And a chart whose rows are separate bars has to give each bar a label of its own. The charts the issue names were read for that:
  - Person Analytics reads its table's Chart label column and Archival Analytics its ranking's `label`, both already made unique for the chart's axis. Regions, countries, kinds of collection and degree buckets are distinct by what they are.
  - **Both administration charts** drew two bars under "Grover Cleveland": his two terms were not consecutive, and the shipped index populates both. Their graphs now name each bar by `ChartInspectorAdapters.administrationGraphLabels(_:)`: the president's name, and the year the term began where another administration in the table has the name ("Grover Cleveland 1885", "Grover Cleveland 1893"), as the chart's own axis tells them apart ("Cleveland 1885"). The name is composed from the name and the year and has no key.
  - **Most-Referenced Documents** names an indexed document by its printed head, and heads repeat: the chart's own doc comment records four "Department of State Minutes" in one ranking. `AnalyticsChartTables.crossRefRankingTable` now states its graph, each bar under the name the chart's axis prints for it (`disambiguatedRankingLabels`, with the three values the chart gives it). Its Document column, in the table and the CSV, is unchanged.
- **Two repeats are left.** *Citation forms across your volumes* is one bar for each era, stacked by kind of file, and its card reads the table's rows as one series: each era holds one point for each kind, and no point says which kind. That was so before, when the axis listed the era once for every row. What it needs is a series for each kind. And Corpus Analytics ▸ By Volume labels a volume by its manifest title, which two of the 553 share (`frus1877`, `frus1877app`).
- **Not heard on a device.** A simulator plays no Audio Graph. The fix follows the header, and `CategoricalAudioGraphPointTests` holds each point to it. The owner's listen is the plan's §3.

**The Copy button for the language-analysis record (#1608)**
- `NaturalLanguageReadiness.record(_:)`, the one place a line goes to the release log, also keeps it, with the time it was written, in the process's `SessionRecord`: at most 200 lines, the first 8 never dropped (a launch's start and verdict, and what was lost), then the most recent; what falls between is counted, and the text says how many in their place. An engine a test builds from fakes writes nothing there.
- Settings ▸ Data & Recovery ▸ Diagnostics ▸ Language Analysis gains a row, **Copy Language Analysis Record**, on iPhone, iPad and Mac (`LanguageAnalysisRow`). It reads *Copied* for two seconds after a press, and VoiceOver is told. It is always enabled: before the first check a record says "no line written yet in this session".
- What it copies (`LanguageAnalysisRecordReport`): a title; four lines the brief did not ask for (the app's version and build, the system's version, the device's model class, and the time of the copy); then each line as `logLine(for:)` wrote it, under its own time to the millisecond with its offset from UTC. The first three carry the four values the Sync Log stamps its rows with (`SyncDiagnosticsLog`, whose four constants are internal now). They are there because the first thing read from the owner's own log was which build had written it. The text is not localised, as Copy Report's is not. It holds enums, scheme names, counts and seconds, and nothing the reader wrote or read.
- The device line is the processor's architecture, `arm64`, on a Mac and in a simulator, as it is in the Sync Log.

**What was looked at.** Every look below was made on the build of `12e5d776`. What changed after it is doc comments, tests, documents, and the names an Audio Graph gives its bars, none of which a screen shows.

**Seen on the iPhone 17 simulator, iOS 27.0, with 1961–1963 vol. III added for the look**
- Language Analysis, on a launch made with `FRUS_DEBUG_NO_LEMMA_ANSWER=1`: *Limited — Not working right now: dictionary forms.
